title: Tricky Deal
summary: Use bishop checks to move the king, then block the rook’s rank with a bishop supported by the promotion pawn.

nodes.question: How can a dark-squared bishop overcome a rook on a light square?
nodes.explanation: The bishop cannot attack e8 directly. Look for a way to block the rook’s line to a8.

branches.title: Check first, then block the rook
commentary: The study starts after Black’s rook has reached e8. The white king has been checked back to d2. Direct promotion gives up the win.
Bf2+ checks along f2-e3-d4. White improves the bishop with tempo instead of trying to attack e8.
Ke5 is forced: the d3 pawn covers c4 and e4, the bishop covers c5 and e3, and d5 is occupied by Black’s pawn.
Bg3+ checks again along g3-f4-e5. The bishop now has a route to b8 along f4-e5-d6-c7.
Kf5 is the illustrated retreat. It vacates the diagonal the bishop needs to reach b8.
Bb8 blocks the eighth rank between the rook and a8. The pawn on a7 protects the bishop on b8.
Rxb8 removes the blocker, but sacrifices the rook onto a square the pawn can capture.
axb8=Q recaptures with promotion. White has exchanged a bishop and pawn for a rook and a queen, retaining a verified win.
branches.explanation: axb8=Q recaptures with promotion. White has exchanged a bishop and pawn for a rook and a queen, retaining a verified win.

branches.title: Test a different king retreat
commentary: Test whether the same interference idea survives another legal response to the bishop check.
Ke5 is the only legal king answer.
Bg3+ opens the route toward b8 while checking.
Kd4 is another legal retreat. It also clears e5, so the bishop’s long diagonal is available.
Bb8 still blocks the rook’s line to a8 and is protected by the a7 pawn.
Rxb8 is a representative way to remove the blocker; it allows a capture with promotion.
axb8=Q reaches another verified White win. The important condition was clearing the diagonal, not the king choosing exactly f5.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: axb8=Q reaches another verified White win. The important condition was clearing the diagonal, not the king choosing exactly f5.

branches.title: Try promoting immediately
commentary: The pawn is ready to promote, but the rook already watches a8 along the eighth rank.
a8=Q promotes without removing that defense. White has traded away the forcing bishop maneuver and gives up the forced win.
Rxa8 captures the queen. The remaining bishop-and-pawn position is a tablebase draw with best play.
branches.explanation: Rxa8 captures the queen. The remaining bishop-and-pawn position is a tablebase draw with best play.

exercises.prompt: What does Bb8 achieve that attacking e8 cannot?
exercises.answer: It interferes with the rook’s line to a8. Since a7 protects b8, capturing the bishop allows axb8=Q.

exercises.prompt: Why use two checks before blocking the rook?
exercises.answer: The checks bring the bishop to g3 and move the king away from e5, clearing the g3-f4-e5-d6-c7-b8 diagonal.

startContext: Begin after the rook checks have driven White’s king to d2 and Black has played ...Re8. This study verifies the final bishop maneuver and contrasts it with immediate promotion.
verification_scope: Selected positions reconstructed from saved source images. Every encoded move and intermediate outcome is checked; representative replies illustrate the idea without enumerating every legal defense.
